title: The Caucasus between Byzantium and Persia
subtitle: AD 428–645 · The Marzbans, Avarayr, the Lazic War, the Georgian Alphabet and the First Arab Raids

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Persian marzbans and the Mamikonian and Bagratuni leaders, the Byzantine province of Armenia, Vakhtang Gorgasali and the erismtavari of Kartli, Albania's Vachagan, and Lazica

entries.label: The Persian marzbans of Armenia
entries.hint: After the nobles had asked the Persians to depose the last Arsacid in 428, Armenia was governed by a Persian marzban from Dvin, with the Armenian aristocracy keeping its lands and sparapet. Appointed marzbans, Persian and in some periods Armenian, directed taxes, fire temples and the army until the Byzantine gains of the 590s.
entries.note: Yeghishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar of Parpi, History; Nina Garsoïan in R. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 1 (1997).

entries.label: Vardan and Vahan Mamikonian
entries.hint: Vardan Mamikonian, sparapet, led the Armenian nobles in the rising of 450–451 against Yazdegerd II's order to adopt Zoroastrianism and fell at Avarayr; his nephew Vahan Mamikonian led a successful guerrilla war in 481–484 and was appointed marzban in 485, a post he held until his death about 510. The family became the leading house of Persian Armenia.

entries.label: Smbat Bagratuni, 'Khosrow Shum'
entries.hint: Smbat IV Bagratuni, called Khosrow Shum, served Khosrow II as a Persian general and marzban of Vrkan (Hyrcania), where Sebeos says he defeated the Kushans in a great battle, and was the symbol of the rise of his house in the Persian service. The Bagratunis would later rule Armenia as kings.

entries.label: Justinian's Armenia
entries.hint: Justinian reorganised the empire's small share of Armenia: in 528 he put the Byzantine provinces under a magister militum per Armeniam at Theodosiopolis (Erzurum), and in 536 divided them into Armenia I–IV, ended the local houses' independent succession rights, and fortified the frontier. The measure provoked Armenian revolt in 538–539.
entries.note: Procopius, Buildings 3.1–4; Wars 2.3; Justinian, Novels 21, 31 (536); Garsoïan 1997.

entries.label: Maurice and the partition of 591
entries.hint: Following the aid of Maurice to restore the Persian king Khosrow II, the peace of 591 moved the Byzantine frontier east, giving Byzantium most of Armenia west of a line running through Lake Van and the Hrazdan, and a large part of Iberia; Maurice then moved thousands of Armenian soldiers to the Balkans and Thrace.

entries.label: Vakhtang Gorgasali
entries.hint: Vakhtang I, called Gorgasali ('wolf-head'), is the king of Georgian tradition who built Tbilisi, led the revolt against Persia in 482–484, moved his seat from Mtskheta to Tbilisi and obtained autocephaly for the Georgian Church. The chronicle's date for his death is 522; some historians put it in 502. The Life of Vakhtang was composed some centuries after him.
entries.note: Juansher, Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali (in Kartlis Tskhovreba); Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963); Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

entries.label: The end of the monarchy and the erismtavari
entries.hint: After Vakhtang the Iberian kings fell increasingly under Persian control, and about 580 Hormizd IV is said to have abolished the royal office; the Georgian chronicle names its rulers from Guaram I (c. 588) as erismtavari, 'prince of princes', confirmed by Byzantium as curopalates. Stephen I (c. 590–627) built the Jvari church and died in the war with Heraclius.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Procopius, Wars 1.12; Toumanoff 1963; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Vachagan the Pious and the Albanian kings
entries.hint: Vachagan III, called the Pious, king of Albania under Persian suzerainty from about 485, held in 488 the council of Aghuen to organise the Albanian church, appears as a vassal of Kavadh I and his successors, and the capital moved to Partaw in the plain; the Albanian monarchy lasted until 510 and then continued under governors.
entries.note: Movses Kaghankatvatsi, History of the Albanians 1.26, 1.27; Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

entries.label: Lazica (Egrisi)
entries.hint: In the sixth century the kingdom of Lazica in western Georgia, known to its people as Egrisi, was a client state of Byzantium under its king Tzath (Tzath's baptism at Constantinople in 522) and his successors, in which Justinian built the fort of Petra, and which Persia tried to seize as an outlet to the Black Sea. The Lazic War of 541–562 was fought on its territory.

entries.label: The Mihranids of Albania
entries.hint: In about 630 Varaz-Grigor of the Persian Mihranid house, with the support of Byzantium, took the princely title in Albania as a client of both powers, beginning the Mihranid dynasty (Girdman), which was to rule through the Arab conquest.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Avarayr, Vahan's rising, the Armenian revolt of 571, the Lazic War, Heraclius and the Khazars at Tiflis, and the first Arab raids

entries.label: Avarayr
entries.hint: In 451 Yazdegerd II ordered the Armenians to give up Christianity for the religion of Mazda; the nobles under Vardan Mamikonian rose and on 26 May met the Persian army on the plain of Avarayr, where Vardan and many chiefs were killed and the Persians prevailed. The Armenian Church honours the dead as the Vardanank martyrs, and the date is among the great feasts.
entries.note: Yeghishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar of Parpi; Garsoïan 1997.

entries.label: Vahan Mamikonian's war
entries.hint: Armenians and Iberians, led by Vahan Mamikonian and King Vakhtang, rose against Persia in 481 when Peroz sought to force Zoroastrianism; after the Persian defeat and death of Peroz in 484 against the Hephthalites, the new king Valash concluded the treaty of Nvarsak. Vahan was made marzban.

entries.group: The Lazic War and the Roman–Persian Wars
entries.label: The Lazic War
entries.hint: In 541 the Lazic king Gubazes, resenting Byzantine oppression, called in Khosrow I, who took Petra the next year and made Lazica a Persian protectorate; Gubazes returned to the Byzantines and the war went on for two decades, with Roman victories at Archaeopolis (551) and Phasis (555). Procopius and Agathias are the main historians.

entries.group: The Lazic War and the Roman–Persian Wars
entries.label: The murder of Gubazes
entries.hint: In 555 the Roman generals Martin and Rusticus, who had quarrelled with King Gubazes II, killed him at a banquet; the Lazi, who had to be placated by Justinian's enquiry and the punishment of Rusticus and John, continued in alliance. Agathias gives a detailed account of the murder and of the trial.

entries.label: The rising of 571
entries.hint: In 571 the Persian marzban's attempt to build a fire temple at Dvin led the Armenians, under Vardan Mamikonian, to kill him; they sought the aid of Justin II, which brought on the Roman–Persian war of 572–591, in which the Armenians of Dvin fought on the Roman side.
entries.note: Sebeos 3; Menander Protector fr. 9; Evagrius 5.7; John of Ephesus.

entries.group: The Lazic War and the Roman–Persian Wars
entries.label: Heraclius and the Khazars at Tiflis
entries.hint: In 627 the emperor Heraclius, after campaigning in Albania and Armenia against Khosrow II, joined the Turkic Khazar khagan, who is said to have brought 40,000 horsemen, in the siege of Tbilisi, which fell; the Persian partisan Stephen I of Iberia was killed. The campaign led to the battle of Nineveh.
entries.note: Theophanes, Chronicle AM 6113–6117; Movses Kaghankatvatsi 2.12; Sebeos 41; Kartlis Tskhovreba.

entries.group: The Last War and the Arabs
entries.label: The first Arab raids and the fall of Dvin
entries.hint: In 640 an Arab army from Syria, and again in 642, entered Armenia; at Dvin, after a siege, it took the city on 6 October 640, killed according to Sebeos 12,000 and took 35,000 captives. Theodoros Rshtuni and the Mamikonians would later come to terms. These raids were the first stage of the Arab conquest of the Caucasus.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The treaty of Nvarsak, Justinian's Armenian reform, the Fifty Years' Peace and the peace of 591

entries.label: The treaty of Nvarsak
entries.hint: After the rising of 481–484 the Persian king Valash accepted Vahan Mamikonian's terms at Nvarsak: the Armenians' Christian worship and church would be respected, no fire temples would be forced on them, and Armenians would hold office under the Persian king in their own land. It was the Armenian aristocracy's charter in the Persian period.

entries.label: The Persian tax survey and the marzban's court
entries.hint: The tax reform of Khosrow I, with a survey of land, a fixed land tax and a poll tax, was applied in the empire's provinces, presumably including Persarmenia, where the marzban's court at Dvin would have overseen assessment and collection while the nobles continued to supply cavalry.
entries.note: Tabari, Annals (on Khosrow Anushirvan's reforms); Sebeos; Garsoïan 1997.

entries.label: Justinian's laws for Armenia
entries.hint: Justinian's Novel 21 and Novel 31 of 536 divided the Roman part of Armenia into four provinces, put an end to the custom by which Armenian lands passed by the male line only and gave daughters equal inheritance as in Roman law. The measure caused a revolt in 538–539 and the killing of the governor Acacius.

entries.label: The Fifty Years' Peace
entries.hint: The treaty of 562 between Justinian and Khosrow I recognised Byzantine control of Lazica, to be cleared of Persian troops, in return for an annual payment of 30,000 solidi to Persia, and provided for the freedom of Christians in Persia. The text is preserved by Menander the Guardsman.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The council of Dvin and the rejection of Chalcedon, the break of 607, the Iberian church and the Albanian council of Aghuen

entries.label: Yazdegerd II's edict and the martyrs
entries.hint: Yazdegerd II, whose chief minister Mihr-Narseh urged him to unify the empire in the religion of Mazda, ordered the Armenians, Iberians and Albanians in 449 to give up Christianity; the nobles pretended to comply and then rose. The edict is the main case in the Caucasus of a Sasanian attempt at religious unity.

entries.label: The Iberian church and Peter the Iberian
entries.hint: The Iberian church had a head at Mtskheta, who in Vakhtang's time won the rank of Catholicos with the Antiochene patriarch's consent; the Iberian prince Peter, a hostage at Constantinople, became bishop of Maiuma near Gaza and a leader of the anti-Chalcedonians, with a Life by John Rufus.
entries.note: John Rufus, Life of Peter the Iberian; Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The council of Aghuen
entries.hint: The Albanian council held at Aghuen in 488 under King Vachagan III and the Albanian bishops issued twenty-one canons for the Albanian church on the clergy, marriage, burial, dealings with the sorcerers and the tithe. The text, preserved in an Armenian history, is a unique record of this church's discipline.
entries.note: Movses Kaghankatvatsi, History of the Albanians 1.26; Hewsen 2001.

entries.label: The rejection of Chalcedon at Dvin
entries.hint: The first council of Dvin in 506 under the Catholicos Babken, attended by Armenian, Iberian and Albanian bishops, endorsed the 'Henotikon' of Zeno and rejected the Council of Chalcedon, whose dyophysite formula was taken to be Nestorian; a second council in 554 reaffirmed this. The Armenian Church thereby took the miaphysite position it still holds.

entries.label: The break of 607
entries.hint: At the third council of Dvin in 607 the Catholicos Abraham of Armenia expelled the Iberian bishop Kyrion and his church, which had accepted Chalcedon, so that the Georgian and Armenian churches separated, a division which has lasted. The dispute shaped each nation's identity.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The domed churches of Armenia, Bolnisi Sioni and Jvari, and the mosaic of Bir el Qutt

entries.label: The mosaic of Bir el Qutt
entries.hint: A monastery church floor discovered in 1952 near Bethlehem carries a dedication in Georgian, with the names of Iberian founders, in Asomtavruli letters, and is the oldest dated Georgian inscription known, of the first half of the fifth century. It is the first firm evidence for the use of the alphabet.

entries.label: The early Armenian churches
entries.hint: In the fifth to seventh centuries Armenian masons built basilicas, such as Ereruyk and Tekor, and domed centralised buildings, such as Ptghni and Avan, in dressed local stone and with barrel vaults, a style that came to be distinctive. Hripsime (618), Gayane (630) and Mren (about 640) are inscribed with their founders.
entries.note: Hripsime and Mren church inscriptions; Garsoïan 1997; Sirarpie Der Nersessian, Armenian Art (1977).

entries.label: Bolnisi Sioni
entries.hint: The basilica of Bolnisi Sioni, a three-aisled church of cut stone, was built between 478 and 493, and carries the oldest dated Georgian inscription in Georgia itself, of 493–494. It is the best early example of the Georgian basilica.
entries.note: Bolnisi Sioni inscription; Georgian National Museum; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Jvari
entries.hint: On the hill at the confluence of the Aragvi and Kura, the Jvari church, 'of the Cross', was built about 590–605 by Stephen I and his successors on the spot where Nino had set up a cross; it is a tetraconch with a dome on squinches, and its type was copied in Armenia and Georgia. UNESCO lists it with Mtskheta.
entries.note: Jvari inscriptions; UNESCO World Heritage no. 708 (1994); Rapp 2003.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Georgian alphabet, Shushanik's martyrdom, the historians of Vardan, Procopius on Lazica and the Armenian era

entries.label: The Georgian alphabet
entries.hint: The Georgian script in its first form, Asomtavruli, is first seen in the inscriptions of Bir el Qutt (about 430) and Bolnisi (493). Its origin is debated: Georgian tradition ascribed it to King Pharnavaz, Armenian sources to the circle of Mesrop, and many scholars see it as a fifth-century creation influenced by Greek and Aramaic letters.
entries.note: Bir el Qutt and Bolnisi inscriptions; Koriun, Life of Mashtots 16; Rapp 2003; Wolfgang Schulze et al.

entries.label: The historians of Vardan
entries.hint: Yeghishe, with his History of Vardan and the Armenian War, and Lazar of Parpi, with a History for the Mamikonian Vahan, wrote the account of the risings in the best classical Armenian prose and gave the events the shape of a martyrs' narrative. Both are in the golden age of the Armenian language.
entries.note: Yeghishe, History of Vardan; Lazar of Parpi, History.

entries.label: The Martyrdom of Shushanik
entries.hint: Iakob Tsurtaveli, her priest, wrote down within a few years of her death the life of Shushanik, daughter of the Armenian Vardan Mamikonian and wife of the Iberian prince Varsken, who gave up Christianity and was killed for resisting; it is the oldest surviving original work of Georgian literature.
entries.note: Iakob Tsurtaveli, The Martyrdom of Shushanik; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Procopius on Lazica
entries.hint: Procopius, secretary of Belisarius, gives in the Wars and in Buildings a detailed account of Lazica, its climate and products, its wars with Persia, and of the Caucasus; Agathias, a lawyer, continues it to 559. These are the main literary records of the western Caucasus in this age.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.15, 8.1–17; Procopius, Buildings 3; Agathias, Histories.

entries.label: The Armenian era and Movses Khorenatsi
entries.hint: The Armenian church adopted in 552 a calendar of its own, counted from 11 July 552, the era used in Armenian documents; the History of Armenia attributed to Movses Khorenatsi, ascribed to the fifth century, is thought by some scholars to be a work of the late seventh or eighth century. The dating of the work remains a major dispute.
entries.note: Council of Dvin (554/555); Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians (trans. R. Thomson, 1978); Garsoïan 1997.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Hides, slaves and honey from Lazica, the markets of Dvin and the Persian tax survey

entries.label: Dvin, the market of the highlands
entries.hint: Dvin was both the seat of the marzban and a great trading town on the roads to the Black Sea and Persia, with a population of Armenians, Persians, Syrians and Jews; its market, according to later sources, drew merchants from far. Excavations show craftsmen's quarters, glass and ceramics made on the spot.

entries.label: Lazica's hides, slaves and honey
entries.hint: Procopius tells that Lazica had neither grain nor wine and no other produce of its own, and that the Lazi exchanged hides, skins, slaves and honey with the Romans for salt, grain and other goods, and the Roman merchants came in boats to Apsarus and Phasis. The exchange gave Byzantium its interest in the country, and was the basis of the monopolies of Justinian's officials.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Sasanian walls of the Caspian gate, the fortress of Petra and the Armenian dome

entries.label: The Sasanian walls of the Caucasus
entries.hint: To close the passes between the Caspian and the mountains against steppe nomads, the Sasanian kings, Peroz, Kavadh I and Khosrow I, built a system of walls and forts. The Gilgilchay wall, running from the Caspian shore inland for some 50 kilometres in what is now Azerbaijan, and Derbent's walls (in Dagestan, outside this zone) were the best known.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.10; Tabari; Hewsen 2001; Gilgilchay surveys.

entries.label: The Armenian dome on squinches
entries.hint: The builders of the highlands developed a type of domed church of precisely cut stone, with the dome carried on squinches or pendentives over a square or cruciform plan, and walls of rubble faced with ashlar and set in lime mortar. Their method influenced later Byzantine and Islamic architecture.

entries.label: Petra and Archaeopolis
entries.hint: Justinian had the fortress of Petra built on the Black Sea coast near modern Batumi by his general John Tzibus in 535, and it became the base of Byzantine trade and Persian attack; inland the older fortress of Archaeopolis, identified with Nokalakevi in Georgia, was besieged by the Persians in 551 without success. Nokalakevi has been under excavation since 1973.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Armenians in the Byzantine army, Narses, and the Khazar alliance

entries.label: Armenians in the Byzantine army
entries.hint: Armenian nobles and soldiers served in large numbers in Byzantine armies, from the eunuch general Narses, who completed Justinian's reconquest of Italy, to the cavalry units that Maurice moved to the West. Armenia was a main recruiting ground, and the emperor Heraclius was himself, according to Armenian sources and many modern historians, of Armenian descent.

entries.label: The Khazar alliance
entries.hint: Heraclius made an alliance with the western Turkic ruler of the Khazars, Ziebel, who in 626–627 joined him in the siege of Tbilisi; the emperor promised his daughter in marriage and gave rich gifts. It was the first of many Khazar contacts with Byzantium and the south Caucasus.
entries.note: Theophanes AM 6113, 6117; Nikephoros, Breviarium 12; Movses Kaghankatvatsi 2.12.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The plague, the exhausting wars of Persia and Byzantium and the opening of the Arab conquests

entries.label: The plague and the wars of exhaustion
entries.hint: The plague that came to the Mediterranean in 541–542 spread east to Persia and Mesopotamia and probably reached the Caucasus, and the long wars between Byzantium and Persia, which culminated in the war of 602–628, devastated the borderlands and left both empires weak. The Arab conquests followed within a decade.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A saint married to a persecutor, the captives of Dvin and the Armenian cavalryman

entries.label: Shushanik
entries.hint: Shushanik, an Armenian princess married to the Iberian prince Varsken, refused to follow him in renouncing Christianity for the Persian religion, was beaten, imprisoned for six years and died in prison; her priest's account makes her the first Georgian saint. Her story shows the pressure of the Persian court on noble families.

entries.label: The Armenian cavalryman
entries.hint: The Armenian horseman, from the nakharar retinue or the royal levies, appears in Procopius, Agathias and Sebeos as an expert archer and lancer, paid in the Byzantine pay lists and sometimes serving in Persian ones; many of the common soldiers' lives were passed far from home in Italy, Africa and the Balkans.

entries.label: The captives of Dvin
entries.hint: Sebeos reports that when the Arabs took Dvin they put some 12,000 to the sword and took 35,000 men and women into captivity, many of them from the families who had taken refuge in the city. The figures are those of an Armenian chronicler and may be exaggerated.
